key_terms.meaning: Twisting effort at the crankshaft, in N·m; measured by a dynamometer and multiplied by speed to give power.
Usable power at the crankshaft: BP = 2πNT/60, with N in rev/s and T in N·m, answer in W.
Power developed inside the cylinder by the gas: IP = (p_mi × L × A × n × N)/60 for the whole engine.
Power lost to friction, pumping and auxiliaries: FP = IP − BP.
Fraction of indicated power that reaches the shaft: η_mech = BP/IP = 1 − FP/IP.
Brake power divided by fuel energy rate: η_bt = BP/(ṁ_f × CV), where ṁ_f is kg/s and CV is J/kg.
Indicated power divided by fuel energy rate: η_it = IP/(ṁ_f × CV).
Fuel mass burned per unit brake work per hour: BSFC = ṁ_f/BP, usually in kg/kWh.
Ratio of actual air drawn per cycle to the theoretical swept volume of air at ambient density.
A fictitious constant pressure that would give the brake work in one cycle: BMEP = BP × 60/(L·A·n·N) with consistent units.
AFR = mass of air ÷ mass of fuel; equivalence ratio φ = (AFR)_stoich/(AFR)_actual, so φ > 1 is rich.
A running test on a multi-cylinder engine: cut one cylinder at a time and read the drop in brake power, which equals that cylinder's indicated power.
A loading device that absorbs engine torque and measures it, giving brake power directly when speed is known.
An account of fuel energy split into brake power, cooling water, exhaust gas and unaccounted losses, all in kJ/min or as percentages.
Heat released by burning unit mass of fuel completely, in kJ/kg; petrol about 44 000 kJ/kg, diesel about 42 500 kJ/kg.
A quartz sensor that turns in-cylinder pressure into a small electric charge for recording against crank angle.
Electronics that convert the tiny charge from a piezoelectric sensor into a proportional voltage for the data logger.
A shaft-mounted disc that gives one pulse per degree (or fraction) of rotation so pressure data can be tagged to crank position.
Rate at which chemical energy of the fuel appears as heat in the cylinder, computed from the pressure–crank-angle record.
A fixed speed–time schedule (for example MIDC or NEDC) that a vehicle follows on a chassis dynamometer so emission results are comparable.

takeaways: Every performance number is built from three measurements only: torque, speed and fuel flow.
Brake power is measured; indicated power is inferred; friction power is the difference between them.
A Morse test separates the cylinders' indicated powers by removing one working cylinder at a time.
Fuel flow and air flow must be logged with the load, because efficiency is meaningless without both.
A dynamometer is a calibrated brake; a test cell makes its reading repeatable and safe.
The heat balance sheet proves that the measured outputs add up to the fuel energy supplied.
Load, speed, AFR, ignition or injection timing, compression ratio and ambient conditions move power and efficiency together.
Performance improves only through more air, better mixture, less friction and better control.
A result is valid only if the test standard, the running-in state and steady or transient condition are stated.
The in-cylinder pressure trace is the richest single record of what happens inside the engine.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are usually numeric plus explanatory: define the parameter with its formula and units, then substitute measured values and comment on whether the efficiency or the heat balance looks reasonable.

bank.q: Define brake power, indicated power and friction power, and derive the relation between them. Show how each is expressed in terms of torque, speed and mean effective pressure.
outline: BP = 2πNT/60 with symbols defined and units stated
IP from indicator diagram or p_mi form
FP = IP − BP and its components (rubbing, pumping, auxiliaries)
η_mech = BP/IP, typical values for SI and CI engines
Statement that BP is measured, IP is inferred

bank.q: Explain the Morse test for a four-cylinder engine. State its assumptions, the procedure, and how indicated and friction power are calculated.
outline: All cylinders firing, note BP at constant speed
Cut one cylinder, reload to same speed, note new BP
Difference equals IP of the cut cylinder
Assumption: IP of remaining cylinders unchanged; constant speed maintained
Sum of individual IPs, FP = total IP − BP

bank.q: Describe the instruments used to measure fuel consumption and air consumption of an engine on a test bed, with the principle of each.
outline: Volumetric fuel measurement and burette with stopwatch, fuel density correction
Fuel flowmeter (rotameter, Coriolis) for continuous reading
Air box with sharp-edged orifice and manometer, Cd value
Venturi nozzle or hot-wire air flow meter
Need for simultaneous logging of fuel and air with load and speed

bank.q: What is a heat balance sheet? List the items on the credit and debit sides and explain how each is evaluated from test data.
outline: Credit side: heat supplied = ṁ_f × CV
Debit: heat to brake power
Heat to cooling water from water flow and temperature rise
Heat to exhaust gas from gas flow, specific heat and temperature rise
Unaccounted losses (radiation, convection, incomplete combustion) as the balance term
Presentation in kJ/min and percentage

bank.q: Explain the construction and working of absorption and eddy-current dynamometers. Why is a transient dynamometer needed for emission testing?
outline: Absorption type: Prony brake, rope brake, hydraulic, eddy current
Torque measurement by reaction arm and load cell
Power = 2πNT/60 from measured torque and speed
Eddy-current: no mechanical friction, fast load control
Transient dynamometer follows a driving cycle with rapid speed and load changes, allowing motoring and regeneration

bank.q: List the engine operating variables that affect performance and state, for any four, the direction of their effect on power, efficiency and emissions.
outline: Speed, load, air–fuel ratio, ignition or injection timing
Compression ratio, valve timing, intake air temperature and density
Coolant and oil temperature, deposits and wear
Fuel quality, altitude and humidity
Direction of effect stated for each chosen variable with reason

bank.q: A four-stroke, four-cylinder engine has bore 80 mm, stroke 110 mm and runs at 3000 rpm. The measured brake torque is 120 N·m. Calculate brake power, swept volume per cylinder, and BMEP.
outline: Swept volume per cylinder = (π/4) × 0.080² × 0.110 ≈ 5.53 × 10⁻⁴ m³
Total swept volume and cycles per second for four-stroke
BMEP = BP × 60/(L·A·n·N) with n = 4 for four-stroke
Consistent SI units and answer in bar

bank.q: An engine develops 40 kW brake power and consumes 11 kg of fuel per hour. The calorific value is 42 000 kJ/kg. Find brake thermal efficiency, BSFC, and the fuel energy rate in kW.
outline: Fuel energy rate = ṁ_f × CV in kW
η_bt = BP/fuel energy rate, expressed as percentage
BSFC = ṁ_f/BP in kg/kWh
Comment on whether the value is realistic for a CI engine

bank.q: In a Morse test on a four-cylinder engine running at constant speed, the brake power with all cylinders firing is 30 kW. Successive cut-outs give 22.5, 22.8, 22.6 and 22.4 kW. Find the indicated power of each cylinder, total IP, friction power and mechanical efficiency.
outline: Each IP = BP(all firing) − BP(with that cylinder cut)
IP values 7.5, 7.2, 7.4, 7.6 kW
Total IP = 29.7 kW
FP = IP − BP = −0.3 kW, so state that a negative or near-zero value indicates experimental error or that the brake load was not restored to the same speed
η_mech = BP/IP and comment on accuracy of the Morse test

bank.q: During a one-hour test an engine used 8 kg of fuel of calorific value 43 000 kJ/kg and produced 30 kW brake power. Cooling water flow was 15 kg/min with a 12 °C rise, exhaust gas flow 9 kg/min with a 400 °C rise, specific heat 1.0 kJ/kg·K. Prepare the heat balance in kJ/min and in percent.
outline: Heat supplied per minute from fuel rate and CV
Heat to brake power = BP × 60 kJ/min
Heat to water = ṁ_w × c_p × ΔT with c_p = 4.18 kJ/kg·K
Heat to exhaust = ṁ_g × c_p × ΔT
Unaccounted = supplied − (all three)
Percentages and comment that unaccounted should be positive and modest

bank.q: A sharp-edged orifice of 30 mm diameter in an air box passes air when the head across it is 60 mm of water. Ambient air density is 1.2 kg/m³ and the coefficient of discharge is 0.62. Find the air mass flow rate, and the volumetric efficiency of a 1.5 litre four-stroke engine running at 2500 rpm if it consumes this air.
outline: Δp = ρ_water × g × h
Velocity from orifice equation with Cd
ṁ_air = Cd × A × velocity × ρ_air
Theoretical air per second = (V_s/2) × (N/60) for four-stroke
η_v = actual/theoretical, expressed as percentage

bank.q: Indicated power cannot be measured directly on a production engine. Compare the precision, assumptions and limitations of the Morse test, the motoring test and the use of a cylinder pressure transducer for obtaining IP.
outline: Morse test: running engine, assumes unchanged IP of other cylinders, sensitive to speed control
Motoring test: gives friction only, loses combustion and pumping fidelity, cannot run fired
Pressure transducer: direct p–V integration, needs crank-angle referencing and absolute pressure correction
Comparison of accuracy, cost, time and applicability
Recommendation depending on purpose (development versus routine check)

bank.q: Evaluate the methods available to improve engine performance and rank them by their effect on brake thermal efficiency and emissions.
outline: Four levers: more air, better mixture, less friction, better control
Turbocharging and intercooling for trapped air mass
Fuel injection pressure, spray and mixture preparation, direct injection
Friction reduction: low-tension rings, coatings, variable oil pump, fewer cylinders for same power
Control: variable valve timing, electronic timing and closed-loop AFR, cylinder deactivation
Trade-off discussion: gains in efficiency against NOx and particulate emissions
Justified ranking

bank.q: Discuss why an emission or power figure is meaningless unless the test standard, driving cycle and running-in condition are stated. Include the difference between gross and net power and between steady-state and transient testing.
outline: Need for agreed procedure: ambient correction, fuel specification, auxiliaries fitted
Gross power with only essential auxiliaries versus net power as installed
Running-in: friction falls and power stabilises over the first hours
Steady-state test cells versus transient chassis dynamometer tests
Driving cycles: MIDC, NEDC, their purpose and their limits of realism
Cycle-to-cycle variation and logging requirements for valid data

glossary.def: A dynamometer that converts the absorbed engine power into heat, as in water-brake and eddy-current types.
A large settling chamber fitted with an orifice or nozzle, used to measure the air drawn by an engine smoothly and steadily.
Brake mean effective pressure, the constant pressure that would produce the measured brake work in one cycle.
Brake specific fuel consumption, the fuel mass needed per kilowatt-hour of brake work.
The Indian Bharat Stage VI emission norm, applied to new vehicles from 2020, with tight limits on NOx, particulate matter and sulphur in fuel.
An electronic unit that converts the charge from a piezoelectric sensor into a proportional voltage.
An emission instrument that measures oxides of nitrogen by the light emitted when NO reacts with ozone.
The scatter in peak pressure and work between successive cycles of the same cylinder under identical settings.
A dynamometer that loads the engine by electromagnetic drag with no mechanical contact, allowing fast control.
An instrument that measures hydrocarbon concentration by ionising the sample in a hydrogen flame.
Power measured with only the auxiliaries essential for running; net power is measured with the full installation.
The rate of chemical energy release during combustion, calculated from the cylinder pressure trace.
A statement showing how the fuel energy supplied is divided between brake power, cooling, exhaust and unaccounted losses.
Recording several channels of test data, such as pressure, crank angle, flow and temperature, together with a common time base.
The Modified Indian Driving Cycle, the speed–time schedule used in India for chassis dynamometer emission tests.
A test in which an external motor drives the engine without fuel to measure its friction and pumping losses.
The New European Driving Cycle, a speed–time schedule for vehicle emission testing consisting of urban and extra-urban phases.
An instrument that measures carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide from their absorption of infrared light.
The simplest absorption dynamometer, using friction on a drum and a measured reaction arm.
The initial period of engine operation in which surfaces bed in, friction falls and performance stabilises.
An instrument that measures exhaust opacity or filter blackening to estimate soot from a diesel engine.
A test condition in which speed, load and temperatures are held constant for long enough for all readings to settle.
The minimum air mass per unit fuel mass needed for complete combustion; about 14.7 for petrol and 14.5 for diesel.
A controlled room with a dynamometer, cooling, ventilation, fuel supply and instrumentation for repeatable engine testing.
The ratio of the air actually trapped per cycle to the swept volume of air at ambient conditions.
